title: Figs on a fig tree
hookLine: it's silly to be surprised that a fig tree bears figs (Meditations 8.15)
last: TURN BACK TO WHAT YOU CAN DO.

cards: Your uncle, the one who always brings up politics at dinner, brings up politics at dinner. Your coworker, the one who's always late, is late.
The airline loses your bag, the toddler spills the juice, and the friend who never texts back doesn't. And every time there's a little jolt of outrage, as if this were brand new.
Marcus Aurelius thought the jolt was the odd part. In book eight he compares it to walking up to a fig tree and being shocked to find figs.

teach.b: In Meditations eight, fifteen, Marcus says it would be shameful to be surprised that a fig tree bears figs, and just as shameful to be surprised when the world bears the fruit it bears.
Rudeness, lateness, lost bags: this is what this world, and these people, grow. Then two more pictures.
A doctor shouldn't be surprised that a patient has a fever. A ship's pilot shouldn't be surprised that the wind turns against him.
Fevers and headwinds are their whole job; being shocked by them would make them worse at it. Marcus isn't saying the uncle is right, or that lateness doesn't matter.
He's moving your reaction from surprise to readiness. Expect the fig, and you can plan around it: bring a topic to steer the dinner, tell your coworker the meeting starts ten minutes early.
The doctor treats the fever because she expected fevers. And there's something gentle hidden here. Expecting someone to be themselves is a way of accepting them.

teach.h: THEY'RE NOT DOING IT AT YOU.
teach.b: The fig tree isn't doing figs at you; it's just being a fig tree.
Usually, people aren't doing their habits at you either. Drop the surprise, and a lot of the anger goes with it. What's left is room to respond well, and sometimes even to smile.

how: Readers of Marcus often use the fig tree image to expect familiar behavior in others, which lets them plan a calm response instead of reacting with fresh outrage each time.

o: a sign that a bad season is on its way
the fruit a thing is bound to bear, so no surprise
a small sweet gift that someone offers you

games.q: figs on a fig tree — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus says the uncle's opinions are right because they're natural
he only says not to be surprised; expecting isn't approving.
8.15 uses a doctor and a ship's pilot as examples
neither should be surprised by a fever or a contrary wind.

games.q: your coworker is late to the meeting again. by 8.15, what's the fitting response?
o: expect it, and plan around it calmly.
games.why: Meditations 8.15: it's shameful to be surprised that a fig tree bears figs, or a doctor that a patient has a fever.

practice: Think of someone whose habits regularly annoy you, and picture the habit clearly: the lateness, the opinions, the mess. Now see them as a fig tree and the habit as a fig, of course it's there, and let the surprise drain out.
Then ask: since I know the fig is coming, how could I meet it well?

wordCard.voice: Fig. Marcus says it would be shameful to be surprised that a fig tree bears figs, or that the world bears the fruit it always bears. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a fig, the fruit in Meditations 8.15.

carryVoice: Your line: the wind turns against him. A good pilot is ready for it. See you tomorrow.
